Title: Exact Dynamic Programming for Solow--Polasky Diversity Subset Selection on Lines and Staircases
Text:
Exact Dynamic Programming for Solow–Polasky
Diversity Subset Selection on Lines and Staircases
Michael T. M. Emmerich∗
Faculty of Information Technology
University of Jyväskylä
Jyväskylä, Finland
Abstract
We study exact fixed-cardinality Solow–Polasky diversity subset selection on ordered
finite ℓ1 sets, with monotone biobjective Pareto fronts and their higher-dimensional staircase
analogues as central applications. Solow–Polasky diversity was introduced in biodiversity
conservation, whereas the same inverse-matrix expression appears in metric geometry
as magnitude: for a finite metric space (X, d) with exponential similarity matrix Zij =
e−qd(xi,xj), the quantity 1⊤Z−11 is the magnitude of the scaled finite metric space (X, qd)
whenever the weighting is defined by the inverse matrix. Thus, in this finite exponential-
kernel setting, Solow–Polasky diversity and magnitude are mathematically the same object
viewed through different motivations. Building on the linear-chain magnitude formula of
Leinster and Willerton, we provide a detailed proof of the scaled consecutive-gap identity
SP(X) = 1+P
r tanh(qgr/2), where the gr are the gaps between consecutive selected points.
We then prove an exact Bellman-recursion theorem for maximizing this value over all subsets
of a prescribed cardinality, yielding an O(kn2) dynamic program for an ordered n-point
candidate set and subset size k. Finally, we prove ordered ℓ1 reductions showing that the
same algorithm applies to monotone biobjective Pareto-front approximations and, more
generally, to finite coordinatewise monotone ℓ1 staircases in Rd. These are precisely the
ordered ℓ1 chains for which the Manhattan metric becomes a line metric along the chosen
order, so the one-dimensional dynamic program applies without modification.
Summary
This note records a structured tractable case for fixed-cardinality Solow–Polasky diversity subset
selection. In the finite exponential-kernel setting, the Solow–Polasky value is the magnitude
of the corresponding scaled finite metric space. For ordered points on the line, this matrix
quantity reduces to an additive function of the consecutive selected gaps. This yields an exact
O(kn2) Bellman recursion for selecting k representatives from n ordered candidates. The
same ordered-chain structure also gives an exact bottleneck recursion for minimum pairwise
distance, often called Max–Min Diversity. The same recursion applies to monotone biobjective
Pareto-front approximations under the ℓ1 metric by a one-dimensional distance-preserving
reduction.
Section 1 introduces the Solow–Polasky objective and states explicitly its finite exponential-
kernel equivalence with magnitude of scaled finite metric spaces. It also explains why the
hyperbolic-tangent identity should be viewed as a scaled form of a known result of Leinster and
Willerton rather than as a new identity. Section 2 briefly reviews the origin of Solow–Polasky
diversity, its relation to magnitude, known positive and negative complexity results, and its
use in multiobjective diversity optimization. Section 3 proves the consecutive-gap formula on

Introduction and notation
Let q > 0 and let
X = {x1, . . . , xk} ⊆R
with
x1 < · · · < xk.
The exponential similarity matrix of X is
Z(X) = (Zij)k
i,j=1,
Zij = e−q|xi−xj|.
The Solow–Polasky diversity of X is
SP(X) := 1⊤Z(X)−11.
In the original biological-diversity interpretation, the matrix Z is a similarity matrix and SP(X)
measures an effective number of mutually dissimilar species or alternatives. In metric geometry,
the same expression is known as the magnitude of a finite metric space: if (Y, d) is finite and has
similarity matrix e−d(yi,yj), then its magnitude is 1⊤Z−11 whenever the inverse-matrix weighting
exists. Hence the Solow–Polasky value above is precisely the magnitude of the scaled finite
metric space (X, q| · |). This is the sense in which Solow–Polasky diversity and finite magnitude
are mathematically equivalent in the exponential-kernel setting, although they originate from
different communities and motivations (see also Huntsman [7]).
It is therefore useful to place the formula proved below in its earlier metric-geometric context.
Leinster and Willerton studied the magnitude of finite metric spaces and of compact subsets of
Euclidean space by finite approximation. In their analysis of linear metric spaces, they proved
that a chain with consecutive metric gaps d1, . . . , dk−1 has magnitude 1 + Pk−1
r=1 tanh(dr/2),
and then used this formula in the approximation of the magnitude of a line segment [10,
Theorem 4 and Proposition 6]. After the scaling dr = qgr, their result gives exactly the tanh
formula in Theorem 1. Thus we make no novelty claim for the hyperbolic-tangent identity
itself. The contribution of this note is to translate this magnitude formula into fixed-cardinality
Solow–Polasky subset-selection language, to make the resulting exact Bellman recursion explicit,
to illustrate the ordered ℓ1 reduction on concrete Pareto-front examples, and to record the
corresponding monotone-staircase extension in higher dimensions. We also point out that the
same ordered-chain geometry makes the Bellman recursion exact for minimum pairwise distance,
or Max–Min Diversity, even though the latter is a bottleneck objective rather than an additive
one.
For consecutive points we write
gr := xr+1 −xr > 0,
r = 1, . . . , k −1.
The aim of Section 3 is to prove that for ordered points on the line the value SP(X) depends only
on these consecutive gaps. Section 4 then shows that this turns fixed-cardinality subset selection
into an exact dynamic programming problem. Section 5 proves why the same construction
remains valid for ordered point sets in R2 under the ℓ1 norm and includes two illustrative
Pareto-front examples. Section 6 then formulates the higher-dimensional version in terms of
coordinatewise monotone ℓ1 staircases: after a suitable reindexing, and possibly after reversing
selected coordinate axes, the same ordering sorts all coordinate projections. This is the exact
condition under which the ordered ℓ1 metric is a line metric and the Bellman recursion applies
verbatim.

Related work
Solow–Polasky diversity was introduced in biodiversity conservation as a way to measure the
effective diversity of a collection of species from pairwise similarities or distances, motivated by
statistical comparison arguments rather than only by species counts [12]. In the finite metric
setting used here, with similarity matrix
Zij = e−qd(xi,xj),
the same inverse-matrix expression 1⊤Z−11 is also the magnitude of the scaled metric space
(X, qd), whenever the inverse expression is well-defined. Thus Solow–Polasky diversity is not
merely analogous to magnitude in this setting; it is the finite exponential-kernel instance of
the same mathematical quantity. This connects the biodiversity-conservation indicator to the
broader magnitude and diversity framework of metric geometry and biology [9].
The literature contains both positive and negative algorithmic results, but for closely related
rather than identical optimization problems. Leinster and Meckes studied maximization of
diversity over distributions on a fixed similarity matrix. Their general finite algorithm can be
exponential in the number of species, but they also identify important polynomial-time cases,
including ultrametric matrices and matrices sufficiently close to the identity matrix [9]. These
results are compatible with the present work: they concern diversity-maximizing distributions
for a given set, whereas we study fixed-cardinality subset selection from a candidate set.
For the fixed-cardinality subset-selection problem, recent results show that the general
problem is computationally hard. Emmerich, Pereverdieva, and Deutz prove NP-hardness in
general metric spaces for every fixed kernel parameter q > 0 [6]. A follow-up result strengthens
this by proving NP-hardness even for finite point sets in the Euclidean plane, again for every
fixed positive kernel parameter [5]. The ordered one-dimensional and ordered ℓ1 Pareto-front
cases treated in this note should therefore be read as structured tractable cases rather than as
representative of the unrestricted problem.
Solow–Polasky diversity has also been used in evolutionary multiobjective optimization
and diversity optimization. Ulrich, Bader, and Thiele introduced an indicator-based approach
in which diversity of solution sets is optimized in the context of multiobjective search [13].
More recently, Pereverdieva et al. compared Solow–Polasky diversity with other indicators
for multiobjective diversity optimization, including Max–Min Diversity and Riesz s-Energy
[14], and analyzed properties relevant for subset selection and indicator-based evolutionary
algorithms [11]. Max–Min Diversity, also called the minimum-pairwise-distance criterion, is
closely related to Riesz s-energy: for a fixed finite set, the transformed Riesz quantity

ordered ℓ1 geometry in which an exact dynamic program is available.

Ordered ℓ1 Pareto fronts in the plane
The line result extends exactly to a common two-dimensional Pareto-front setting when distances
are measured in the Manhattan norm.
Theorem 3 (Ordered ℓ1 planar reduction). Let
pi = (ui, vi) ∈R2,
i = 1, . . . , n,
with
u1 < · · · < un
and
v1 > · · · > vn.
8


Thus the points form an ordered monotone chain, for example a mutually non-dominated set
for a bicriteria minimization problem. Define
ti := ui −vi.
Then t1 < · · · < tn and, for every i < j,
∥pj −pi∥1 = tj −ti.
Consequently, for the exponential kernel
Zij = e−q∥pi−pj∥1,
the similarity matrix of the ordered planar set is exactly the similarity matrix of the ordered line
set {t1, . . . , tn}. Hence all formulas from Theorem 1 and the dynamic program from Theorem 2
apply verbatim after replacing yi by ti. In particular, fixed-cardinality Solow–Polasky subset
selection for such ordered ℓ1 point sets is solvable exactly in O(kn2) time and O(kn) memory.
Proof. For i < j, monotonicity of the two coordinates gives
∥pj −pi∥1 = |uj −ui| + |vj −vi| = (uj −ui) + (vi −vj).
Since ti = ui −vi, this equals
(uj −vj) −(ui −vi) = tj −ti.
Moreover, tj −ti = (uj −ui) + (vi −vj) > 0 for i < j, so the ti are strictly increasing. Therefore
the whole ℓ1 distance matrix of the planar chain is identical to the distance matrix of the ordered
line set {t1, . . . , tn}. The Solow–Polasky similarity matrix and objective are functions only of this
distance matrix, so the consecutive-gap formula and Bellman recursion from Theorems 1 and 2
apply without further modification. The complexity bound is inherited from Theorem 2.

Monotone ℓ1 staircases in higher dimensions
The planar reduction in Theorem 3 is a special case of a simple higher-dimensional principle.
The essential requirement is not that the points lie in the plane, but that they can be traversed
without backtracking in any coordinate direction.
Definition 1 (Signed coordinatewise monotone ℓ1 staircase). Let
S = {p1, . . . , pn} ⊂Rd.
We say that S admits an ℓ1-staircase ordering if there exists a permutation π of {1, . . . , n} and
a sign vector
σ = (σ1, . . . , σd) ∈{−1, +1}d
such that, with qi := pπ(i),
σℓq1ℓ≤σℓq2ℓ≤· · · ≤σℓqnℓ
for every ℓ= 1, . . . , d.
Equivalently, after possibly reversing some coordinate axes, the same ordering sorts all coordinate
projections. The associated ℓ1 staircase is the axis-parallel monotone polyline obtained by
connecting consecutive points qi, qi+1 through coordinate-parallel moves.
For σ = (1, . . . , 1) this is an ascending staircase. The two-dimensional Pareto-front case
from Theorem 3 corresponds to d = 2 and σ = (1, −1).

Conclusion and future work
The main conclusion is that fixed-cardinality Solow–Polasky diversity subset selection, although
hard in general metric spaces and even in the Euclidean plane [6, 5], has an exact polynomial-
time solution on ordered one-dimensional sets, on monotone biobjective Pareto fronts under the
ℓ1 metric, and on the higher-dimensional coordinatewise monotone ℓ1 staircases characterized in
Proposition 1. The reason is that the finite exponential-kernel objective becomes the magnitude
of the scaled metric space and, on any ordered ℓ1 chain without coordinate backtracking, this
value is an additive function of the consecutive selected gaps.
Future work should investigate which tractable subclasses remain beyond these coordinate-
wise monotone ℓ1 staircases. Natural directions include partially ordered subsets in Rd that
can be decomposed into a small number of monotone chains, higher-dimensional Pareto-front
structures that are not totally ordered in all coordinate projections, and structural conditions
under which exact recursions, approximation schemes, or useful bounds can be obtained for
Solow–Polasky subset selection.
A related comparison point is Riesz s-energy subset selection in ordered point sets. There,
dynamic-programming ideas can exploit an ordering, but the left–right recurrence considered by
Emmerich is approximate and need not return the exact optimum [4]. The Max–Min Diversity

pairwise distance. On ordered line metrics and on the ℓ1 staircases considered here, that

transition rather than the additive transition used for Solow–Polasky diversity.
Another comparison point is the representation of two-dimensional Pareto fronts of large
cardinality by smaller finite subsets. For the hypervolume indicator and the epsilon-indicator, this
setting has led to algorithms with asymptotically faster running times than the straightforward
left–right dynamic programming used here [2, 8]. In those cases, the optimized measures can be
decomposed into sums of terms that only depend on neighboring selected points. A possible
direction is therefore to ask whether some of these techniques can be translated to Solow–Polasky
diversity subset selection, either to speed up the present recursion or to identify further exactly
solvable ordered and Pareto-front cases. A structurally similar dynamic-programming idea also
appears in the selection of representative points from Pareto fronts for the weighted hypervolume
indicator [1]. This further supports the view that ordered Pareto-front structure can make
otherwise difficult subset selection problems algorithmically tractable.
It is also noteworthy that, for hypervolume subset selection, the hard cases appear when
moving from two-dimensional Pareto-front approximations to three and higher dimensions. In
the anchored-box formulation, Bringmann, Cabello, and Emmerich prove NP-hardness already
in dimension three while retaining polynomial-time solvability in the plane [3]. This contrast
suggests a useful higher-dimensional research direction: to identify precisely which diversity
indicators and geometric structures admit genuinely exact recursions, and which ones require
heuristic or approximation-based dynamic programs.

Abstract: We study exact fixed-cardinality Solow–Polasky diversity subset selection on ordered finite ℓ1 sets, with monotone biobjective Pareto fronts and their higher-dimensional staircase analogues as central applications. Solow–Polasky diversity was introduced in biodiversity conservation, whereas the same inverse-matrix expression appears in metric geometry as magnitude: for a finite metric space (X, d) with exponential similarity matrix Zij = e−qd(xi,xj), the quantity 1⊤Z−11 is the magnitude of the scaled finite metric space (X, qd) whenever the weighting is defined by the inverse matrix. Thus, in this finite exponential- kernel setting, Solow–Polasky diversity and magnitude are mathematically the same object viewed through different motivations. Building on the linear-chain magnitude formula of Leinster and Willerton, we provide a detailed proof of the scaled consecutive-gap identity SP(X) = 1+P r tanh(qgr/2), where the gr are the gaps between consecutive selected points. We then prove an exact Bellman-recursion theorem for maximizing this value over all subsets of a prescribed cardinality, yielding an O(kn2) dynamic program for an ordered n-point candidate set and subset size k. Finally, we prove ordered ℓ1 reductions showing that the same algorithm applies to monotone biobjective Pareto-front approximations and, more generally, to finite coordinatewise monotone ℓ1 staircases in Rd. These are precisely the ordered ℓ1 chains for which the Manhattan metric becomes a line metric along the chosen order, so the one-dimensional dynamic program applies without modification. Summary This note records a structured tractable case for fixed-cardinality Solow–Polasky diversity subset selection. In the finite exponential-kernel setting, the Solow–Polasky value is the magnitude of the corresponding scaled finite metric space. For ordered points on the line, this matrix quantity reduces to an additive function of the consecutive selected gaps. This yields an exact O(kn2) Bellman recursion for selecting k representatives from n ordered candidates. The same ordered-chain structure also gives an exact bottleneck recursion for minimum pairwise distance, often called Max–Min Diversity. The same recursion applies to monotone biobjective Pareto-front approximations under the ℓ1 metric by a one-dimensional distance-preserving reduction. Section 1 introduces the Solow–Polasky objective and states explicitly its finite exponential- kernel equivalence with magnitude of scaled finite metric spaces. It also explains why the hyperbolic-tangent identity should be viewed as a scaled form of a known result of Leinster and Willerton rather than as a new identity. Section 2 briefly reviews the origin of Solow–Polasky diversity, its relation to magnitude, known positive and negative complexity results, and its use in multiobjective diversity optimization.
